title: Robot standards, regulations and certifications: a directory
lead: Robots are covered by standards, laws and certification schemes from many bodies, and the names alone rarely say which one applies to you, whether it is binding, or who can attest to it. This directory is a map. For each entry it says what it is, why it matters, who needs it, how you meet it, who issues or assesses it, and what URML gives you for it.
caveat: It is a starting point, not advice. Which documents apply to a machine depends on what it is, where it works and who buys it; decide that with your risk assessment, a licensed copy of each standard, and, for anything binding, counsel. URML quotes no copyrighted standard text. Editions were checked on the date above; check the publisher's catalogue before relying on a year.

kinds.name: Standard
kinds.what: A consensus document written by a standards body. It says how to do something well: how to design a safe robot cell, how to test a light curtain.
kinds.binding: Not by itself. It becomes binding when a law, a contract or a buyer requires it.

kinds.name: Regulation
kinds.what: Law, or a rule an agency makes under law.

kinds.name: Certification
kinds.what: A third party's statement, after an assessment, that a product, a process or a person meets a document.
kinds.binding: Only as far as a law or a buyer requires it.

kinds.name: Listing or mark
kinds.what: A certification you can see on the product, issued by an accredited lab after testing, such as an NRTL listing to a UL standard.
kinds.binding: Often expected by employers, insurers and local inspectors.

kinds.name: Self-declaration
kinds.what: The maker states conformance and keeps the evidence (the technical file).

kinds.name: Procurement list
kinds.what: A list a buyer uses to admit or exclude vendors and products.
kinds.example: FCC Covered List, DCMA Blue List

roles.name: Standards body
roles.what: Writes and sells the documents. ISO and IEC are international; ANSI is the US member of both and runs the US webstore; A3, UL Standards & Engagement and ISA write US standards; VDA writes industry specifications.

roles.name: Certification body
roles.what: Assesses products, processes or people and issues certificates. The body that writes a standard usually does not certify to it. Named here as examples, not endorsements.

roles.name: NRTL
roles.what: Nationally Recognized Testing Laboratory: a lab OSHA recognizes to test and certify products to listed US safety standards. OSHA publishes which lab may certify to which standard.

roles.name: Authority
roles.what: The agency that makes and enforces a regulation, such as the FAA for drones or the FCC for radio equipment.

roles.name: Notified body
roles.what: In the EU, a conformity assessment body that a Member State has notified to the Commission for a given law. Some machinery, and anything listed in Annex I, Part A of the Machinery Regulation, cannot be assessed by the maker alone and needs one.

terms.what: The analysis of one machine, at one site, in its intended use, that decides which hazards matter, which requirements apply and how strong each safety function must be. Nearly every safety and security standard below starts from it; ISO 12100 says how to do it.

terms.term: Type A, B and C standards
terms.what: Machinery safety standards come in three layers. Type A gives the basic concepts for all machines (ISO 12100). Type B covers one aspect or one kind of safeguard across machines (ISO 13849, ISO 13850, ISO 13855, ISO 14119, IEC 60204-1). Type C is for one kind of machine (ISO 10218 for industrial robots, ISO 3691-4 for driverless trucks). Where a type C standard speaks, it takes precedence.

How strong a function must be. Performance level PLa to PLe (ISO 13849) and safety integrity level SIL 1 to 4 (IEC 62061, IEC 61508) rate safety functions; security level SL 1 to 4 (IEC 62443) rates how much attack a zone must withstand.

How a machine stops: category 0 removes power at once, category 1 brings the machine to a controlled stop and then removes power, category 2 stops under control and keeps power. IEC 60204-1 defines them; an emergency stop uses category 0 or 1.

A function whose failure would raise a risk at once, such as an emergency stop, a protective stop on a light curtain or speed monitoring near people. It lives in the machine's safety-related control, never in URML.
Showing that something meets a document: by the maker's own testing and declaration, by a certification body, or by an accredited lab's listing.

The mark a maker affixes to show a product meets the EU laws that apply to it, after the conformity assessment those laws require. It is not a quality mark and not issued by URML or by a certification body.

support.name: Rulebook template
support.what: Turns a standard's checkable limits into rules the validator enforces before any program runs, and lists the rest as obligations for people. It carries no values from the standard; you fill them in from your risk assessment and licensed copy.

support.name: Runtime
support.what: A URML runtime that speaks the protocol.

support.name: Position page
support.what: Says where URML stands under the standard and what it does not claim.

support.name: Bundled rules
support.what: Checks that ship in the validator and are on by default.

support.name: Ready rulebook
support.what: A rulebook with the law's own citations and nothing to fill in, which you load with --rulebook. Off by default.

support.name: Registry check
support.what: The registry checker enforces a mark's criteria on every entry, and the reproduction run that grants it is public code anyone can repeat.

support.name: Evidence report
support.what: urml evidence build lists, for one deployment, what URML checks for each cited standard and what it leaves to others.

legend.not_a_certifier: URML is never a safety function, a security control or a certifier for anything in this directory. It refuses programs that break declared limits and records what was declared. Certificates come from the bodies named in each entry.

groups.title: Machine safety basics
groups.intro: The standards every machine, robots included, builds on: how to assess risk, how to stop in an emergency, where to put safeguards, how to interlock them, how to wire the machine and how to test the sensors that see people.

entries.name: ISO 12100:2010
entries.title: Risk assessment and risk reduction
entries.who_short: Every machine maker and integrator
entries.what: The basic (type A) machinery safety standard: how to identify hazards, estimate and evaluate risk, and reduce it, first by design, then by safeguards, then by information for use. A second edition is at the draft stage.
entries.why: Every other machinery standard assumes this risk assessment exists. It is the document that decides which requirements, levels and safeguards a robot cell needs, and the first thing an auditor or an inspector asks for.
entries.who: Robot makers, integrators who build cells and lines, and anyone who changes a machine's use.
entries.how: Define the machine's limits and intended use, list the hazards for every task and phase of life, estimate and evaluate each risk, reduce it in the standard's order, and keep the whole analysis on record, updated when anything changes.

assess.text: Reviewed as part of a machine's conformity assessment by certification bodies, or kept by the maker in its technical file.

urml.text: The machinery-safety template refuses programs until the risk assessment's reference is on record, and lists keeping it current as an obligation.

entries.name: ISO 13850:2015
entries.title: Emergency stop function
entries.who_short: Every machine with an emergency stop
entries.what: The principles for designing a machine's emergency stop: what it must do, that it overrides every other function, that it stops in stop category 0 or 1, and that resetting it does not restart the machine. ISO plans a revision.
entries.why: The emergency stop is the last line of protection a person can reach. Robot standards rely on it, and every robot cell has one.
entries.who: Machine and robot makers, and integrators who add emergency stop devices to a cell.
entries.how: Choose the stop category from the risk assessment, design the circuit to the performance level it needs (ISO 13849 or IEC 62061), place and mark the devices, and validate that the stop works and that reset never restarts motion.

assess.text: Part of the machine's conformity assessment; the circuit's safety level is certified with the rest of the safety-related control by bodies such as TÜV SÜD, TÜV Rheinland or UL Solutions.

urml.text: URML never implements, resets or replaces the emergency stop. A program may wait for a declared emergency_stop event; a conforming runtime must stop dispatching and every motion it commands when the substrate reports one (RFC-0701), which the evidence report lists as a runtime obligation. The machinery-safety template asks for the stop category on record and keeps programs off emergency stop outputs.

entries.name: ISO 13855:2024
entries.title: Positioning of safeguards
entries.who_short: Anyone placing light curtains, scanners or guards
entries.what: How far from a hazard a safeguard must be, from the speed at which a person approaches and the machine's total stopping time. Edition 3, replacing the 2010 edition.
entries.why: A light curtain or a scanner field that is too close stops the robot after a person has already reached it. This calculation is where safe distances come from.
entries.who: Integrators who lay out cells and protective fields, and sites that change them.
entries.how: Measure the machine's stopping time, apply the standard's approach speeds and formulas for each safeguard, position the devices, and record and re-verify the calculation after changes.

assess.text: Checked in the machine's validation and conformity assessment.

urml.text: The machinery-safety template refuses programs until the safeguard distance calculation is on record, and lists re-verifying it after changes as an obligation. Lowering a speed limit in the envelope does not change a stopping time URML cannot measure.

entries.name: ISO 14119:2024
entries.title: Interlocking devices associated with guards
entries.who_short: Anyone fitting interlocked doors and guards
entries.what: How to design and choose interlocking devices on guards, such as door switches and guard locks, including how to make them hard to defeat. Edition 3, replacing the 2013 edition.
entries.why: Most robot cells are fenced, and the interlocked door is what stops the robot when someone opens it. Defeated interlocks are a classic cause of accidents.
entries.who: Machine makers and integrators who build guarded cells.
entries.how: Choose the interlock type for each guard, design it to the required performance level, fit it so it is hard to defeat, and validate it.

assess.text: Checked in the machine's validation; interlock devices are often certified by their makers.

urml.text: The machinery-safety template refuses programs until the interlocking record is on file, keeps programs off the outputs that drive guard locks and interlocks, and lists not defeating interlocks as an obligation.

entries.name: IEC 60204-1:2016
entries.title: Electrical equipment of machines
entries.who_short: Anyone building or wiring a machine
entries.what: The requirements for a machine's electrical equipment: supply disconnection, protection, control circuits, wiring, and the stop categories 0, 1 and 2 that emergency stops and protective stops use. Edition 6.0 with Amendment 1:2021.
entries.why: It is the electrical basis every robot cell is wired to, and where the stop categories other standards refer to are defined.
entries.who: Machine and robot makers, panel builders and integrators.
entries.how: Design and build the electrical equipment to the standard, then verify it (continuity, insulation, functional tests) and keep the records.

assess.text: Verified by the maker; certification bodies and NRTLs assess it as part of product certification.

urml.text: The machinery-safety template refuses programs until the electrical verification is on record. URML touches nothing electrical.

entries.name: IEC 61496-1:2020, -3:2025
entries.title: Electro-sensitive protective equipment
entries.who_short: Makers and users of light curtains and safety scanners
entries.what: The requirements and tests for devices that detect people without touching them: part 1 in general, part 3 for laser scanners and other diffuse-reflection devices (2025 edition). Devices are rated by type, 1 to 4.
entries.why: Safety laser scanners on mobile robots and light curtains around cells are how a robot knows a person is near. Their type says how much a fault can be tolerated.
entries.who: Makers of safety sensors; integrators choosing them for a cell or a mobile robot.
entries.how: Choose a device of the type the risk assessment requires, certified to IEC 61496, position it by ISO 13855, and integrate it into the safety-related control.

assess.text: Devices are type-tested and certified by bodies such as TÜV SÜD, TÜV Rheinland or UL Solutions.

urml.text: The machinery-safety template refuses programs until the protective devices' IEC 61496 type is declared and allowed. URML never reads a safety sensor.

groups.title: Robot safety
groups.intro: The machine-specific standards for industrial, collaborative, mobile and personal care robots.

entries.name: ISO 10218-1 and -2:2025, ANSI/A3 R15.06-2025
entries.title: Industrial robots
entries.who_short: Robot makers, integrators, users of industrial robots
entries.what: The safety requirements for industrial robots: part 1 for the robot, part 2 for robot applications and cells. In the US they are adopted as ANSI/A3 R15.06-2025, which replaces R15.06-2012 and adds a US-only part 3 for users.
entries.why: It is the reference a buyer, an insurer, an inspector or a court uses to ask whether an industrial robot cell was made safely. OSHA has no robot-specific standard and looks to consensus standards such as R15.06.
entries.who: Robot makers (part 1), integrators who build cells (part 2), companies that run them (R15.06-3).
entries.how: Risk-assess the cell, design the safeguards and safety functions it calls for, validate them and keep the technical file. Makers usually declare conformance, often backed by a third-party assessment.

assess.text: Certification bodies such as TÜV SÜD, TÜV Rheinland, UL Solutions or SGS.

urml.text: The industrial template: speed and force caps, a program allowlist, untouched safety outputs, the cell layout, the robot's UL 1740 listing on record, and the obligations URML cannot check. Every citation names ISO 10218 and R15.06-2025 together, and two obligations come from R15.06-3 for the people who run the cell: run it as validated, with changes assessed, and train everyone who works with it.

entries.name: ISO/TS 15066:2016
entries.title: Collaborative operation
entries.who_short: Anyone running robots alongside people
entries.what: The technical specification for robots that share space with people: power and force limiting, and speed and separation monitoring. ISO 10218-2:2025 now incorporates its content; a revision is in progress.
entries.why: It is where the limits for contact between a robot and a person come from.
entries.who: Integrators and users of collaborative applications.
entries.how: As for ISO 10218: risk-assess the application, set limits per body region and task, then measure and validate them.

assess.text: The same certification bodies as ISO 10218; force and pressure measurements are often done by them.

urml.text: The force and speed caps in the industrial template; the values come from your licensed copy.

entries.name: ISO 3691-4:2023, ANSI/A3 R15.08
entries.title: Mobile robots and driverless trucks
entries.who_short: Makers and sites running AMRs and AGVs
entries.what: ISO 3691-4:2023 covers driverless industrial trucks and their systems. ANSI/A3 R15.08 is the US standard for industrial mobile robots: part 1 the robot (2020, reaffirmed 2026), part 2 the system and site (2023), part 3 the user (2026).
entries.why: Warehouses and factories run fleets among people; these documents set how the vehicles detect people, slow, stop and stay in their zones.
entries.who: Makers of AMRs and AGVs, integrators, and sites that run them.
entries.how: Risk-assess the site and routes, fit safety-rated personnel detection and speed control, mark the zones, validate, and train the people who work near the robots.

assess.text: Certification bodies such as TÜV SÜD, TÜV Rheinland, UL Solutions or SGS.

urml.text: The AMR template (travel-speed cap, forbidden zones, load handling only at stations, a program allowlist), and the VDA 5050 and ISO 21423 runtimes.

entries.name: ISO 13482:2014
entries.title: Personal care robots
entries.who_short: Makers of service robots that work near people
entries.what: The safety requirements for robots that work close to people outside industry: mobile servants, physical assistants, person carriers. A second edition is in the last stage before publication.
entries.why: It is the main international reference for service robots in homes, care and public spaces.
entries.who: Makers of personal care and service robots.
entries.how: Identify the hazards of the robot in its intended use, assess the risk, then apply the protective measures and validation the standard calls for.

assess.text: Certification bodies such as TÜV SÜD, TÜV Rheinland or UL Solutions.

urml.text: The home template: speed and grip-force caps, hazard zones, no handling in excluded zones. Check its cites when the new edition is out.

groups.title: Functional safety
groups.intro: How the safety functions themselves are designed and rated.

entries.name: ISO 13849-1:2023, -2:2012
entries.title: Safety-related parts of control systems
entries.who_short: Anyone designing safety functions
entries.what: How to design (part 1) and validate (part 2) the parts of a machine's control that perform safety functions, rated by performance level PLa to PLe. A new edition of part 2 is at the final draft stage.
entries.why: An emergency stop, a protective stop or speed monitoring is only as good as its design; the required PL says how good it must be.
entries.who: Machine and robot makers, and integrators who add safety functions.
entries.how: Set the required level (PLr) from the risk assessment, design the architecture, calculate and validate the achieved PL, and document it.

assess.text: Products and components: bodies such as TÜV SÜD, TÜV Rheinland, exida or UL Solutions. People can hold functional-safety certifications too.

urml.text: The functional-safety template: programs wait until each safety function's achieved level is declared and meets the requirement. URML counts toward no PL.

entries.name: IEC 62061:2021
entries.title: Functional safety of machinery
entries.who_short: Designers of electrical safety control
entries.what: The machinery standard for safety-related control, rated by SIL 1 to 3, with Amendment 1:2024 and Amendment 2:2026 (consolidated edition 2.2). A machine is designed to it or to ISO 13849.
entries.why: It is the SIL route to the same goal as ISO 13849, common where electrical and programmable control dominate.
entries.who: Makers and integrators who design safety functions in electrical and programmable control.
entries.how: As for ISO 13849, in the SIL vocabulary.

assess.text: Bodies such as TÜV SÜD, TÜV Rheinland, exida or UL Solutions.

urml.text: The same functional-safety template, which takes SILs.

entries.name: IEC 61508:2010
entries.title: Basic functional safety
entries.who_short: Makers of safety components and safety software
entries.what: The basic functional-safety standard for electrical, electronic and programmable systems, parts 1 to 7, edition 2.0, rated by SIL 1 to 4. IEC 62061 applies it to machinery. Edition 3 is being prepared.
entries.why: Safety controllers, drives with safe torque off and safety-rated sensors are designed and certified to it, and robots outside the machinery standards use it directly.
entries.who: Makers of safety components and of safety-related software.
entries.how: Follow the full safety lifecycle: hazard analysis, safety requirements, design and verification to the target SIL, and, for software, development to IEC 61508-3.

assess.text: Bodies such as TÜV SÜD, TÜV Rheinland, exida or UL Solutions.

urml.text: The functional-safety template (SIL 1 to 4) and a position page: URML is outside the safety-related system and has no SIL.

entries.name: IEC 61800-5-2:2016
entries.title: Safety functions of drives
entries.who_short: Drive makers, and integrators who use a drive's safety functions
entries.what: The functional-safety standard for adjustable speed drives. It names the safety functions a drive can carry out itself, such as safe torque off (STO), safe stop 1 and 2 (SS1, SS2) and safely limited speed (SLS), and rates them in the IEC 61508 and IEC 62061 vocabulary. UL 61800-5-2 is the US version.
entries.why: Most robot stops and speed limits end in the drives. A safety function the drive performs itself is often simpler and faster than one built around it, and its rating feeds the machine's PL or SIL.
entries.who: Makers of drives and servo amplifiers, and integrators who use a drive's safety functions in the machine's safety design.
entries.how: Drive makers design and certify the drive's safety functions to it and publish a safety manual. The integrator configures and validates them in the machine, within the limits that manual sets.

assess.text: Drive makers usually have their drives certified by bodies such as TÜV SÜD, TÜV Rheinland or exida; the integrator validates the configured functions.

urml.text: The functional-safety template: the stop function the drives perform is on record, a speed cap keeps every program below the drives' safely limited speed so none trips it, and programs never write the drives' safety inputs. The drive enforces SLS; URML only avoids asking for more.

groups.title: Security
groups.intro: The cybersecurity of the control system a robot belongs to.

entries.name: IEC 62443
entries.title: Industrial cybersecurity
entries.who_short: Asset owners, integrators, makers of control products
entries.what: ISA/IEC 62443, the series for securing industrial automation and control systems. Most used: 2-1 (the owner's security program), 3-2 (risk assessment, zones and conduits), 3-3 (system requirements, security levels SL 1 to 4), 4-1 (secure development) and 4-2 (component requirements).
entries.why: Robots are networked control systems. Buyers in manufacturing, energy and logistics increasingly ask suppliers for IEC 62443 evidence.
entries.who: Asset owners (2-1, 3-2), integrators (3-3), makers of control products (4-1, 4-2).
entries.how: Model the site as zones and conduits, set target levels from a security risk assessment, meet the system and component requirements, and for products, develop under a 4-1 lifecycle.

assess.text: ISASecure (SDLA for the 4-1 development process, SSA for systems, CSA for components), the IECEE scheme, and certification bodies.

urml.text: The cybersecurity template and a position page mapping URML against the foundational requirements. The VDA 5050 and ISO 21423 runtimes protect their broker conduit with TLS, mutual TLS and broker credentials. URML is not a security control and claims no SL.

groups.title: US product listings
groups.intro: The safety standards a US lab lists a robot to.

entries.name: UL 1740, UL 3100, UL 3300
entries.title: US product listings for robots
entries.who_short: Makers selling robots into US workplaces and public spaces
entries.what: US product safety standards: UL 1740 for robots and robotic equipment, UL 3100 for automated mobile platforms, and UL 3300 for service, communication, information, education and entertainment robots. A robot is tested and listed to one by an NRTL.
entries.why: Employers, insurers and local electrical inspectors in the US often expect equipment to carry an NRTL listing.
entries.who: Makers selling robots into US workplaces and public spaces. Pick the standard by robot type and check its scope.
entries.how: Design to the standard, submit the product to an NRTL for testing, then keep the listing through the lab's follow-up inspections.

assess.text: NRTLs such as UL Solutions, Intertek, TÜV Rheinland or CSA Group; OSHA publishes which lab may certify to which standard.

urml.text: For UL 1740, the industrial template, for robot cells. For UL 3100, the AMR template, for mobile robots at an industrial site. For UL 3300, the service-robot template, for robots in public and commercial spaces. Each keeps programs within the site's limits and refuse them until the listing standard and the NRTL listing are on record. The listing itself covers the robot's hardware and protective functions, which URML does not touch; URML is not part of what the NRTL evaluates.

groups.title: Vocabulary and interoperability
groups.intro: Shared words, and the protocols that let one controller drive robots from many makers.

entries.name: ISO 8373:2021
entries.title: Robotics vocabulary
entries.who_short: Anyone writing about robots precisely
entries.what: The international robotics vocabulary. A fourth edition is at the draft stage.
entries.why: Specifications, contracts and safety files read the same way when they use the same words.
entries.who: Anyone writing requirements, manuals or safety documentation about robots.
entries.how: Nothing to certify; use its terms, from a licensed copy.

assess.text: Not assessed.

urml.text: An alignment page lining up URML's terms with the standard's.

entries.name: VDA 5050 3.0.0
entries.title: Fleet interface for AGVs and AMRs
entries.who_short: Fleet operators and vehicle makers
entries.what: The interface between a fleet controller and driverless vehicles over MQTT, from the German automotive and machinery associations VDA and VDMA. Version 3.0.0 was released in March 2026.
entries.why: One controller can drive vehicles from different makers.
entries.who: Sites running mixed fleets of AGVs or AMRs, and the makers of the vehicles and fleet controllers.
entries.how: Implement the messages and state machine, and test against the official schemas and the other side's implementation. The specification is free; we know of no formal certification scheme for it.

assess.text: No formal scheme we know of; integrators test vehicles against their fleet controller.

urml.text: urml-vda5050-runtime, on PyPI, with TLS and broker credentials on main for the next release, and paid fleet and vehicle validation.

entries.name: ISO 21423:2026
entries.title: Industrial mobile robot interoperability
entries.who_short: Fleet operators and robot makers
entries.what: Communications and interoperability between industrial mobile robots, their fleet managers and site systems, over MQTT. Published in October 2026.
entries.why: As for VDA 5050, as an ISO standard that also covers fleet managers and site equipment.
entries.who: Sites running mobile robots from several makers, robot makers, and fleet manager vendors.
entries.how: Implement it from a licensed copy; we know of no certification scheme yet.

assess.text: No scheme yet that we know of.

urml.text: urml-iso21423-runtime, with TLS and broker credentials, built from public material based on the draft. Validation against the published standard is in progress, and URML makes no conformance claim until it is done.

groups.title: Regulation and procurement
groups.intro: US law for drones, the EU law for machinery, AI and product cybersecurity, and the supply-chain rules for selling to the US government.

entries.name: Regulation (EU) 2023/1230
entries.title: The EU Machinery Regulation
entries.who_short: Anyone placing a robot on the EU market or putting one into service there
entries.what: The EU law for machinery, robots included, from 20 January 2027. It replaces the Machinery Directive 2006/42/EC and sets the essential health and safety requirements, the conformity assessment, the technical file, the EU declaration of conformity and the CE marking. It adds rules for software, protection against corruption and self-evolving behaviour.
entries.why: Machinery sold or used in the EU must meet it. Without the conformity assessment, the declaration and the CE marking, a robot cannot be placed on the market or put into service there.
entries.who: Robot makers and importers, and integrators. Whoever substantially modifies a machine already in service, for example by adding software that creates a new hazard, becomes its manufacturer (Article 18).
entries.how: Carry out the risk assessment, meet the Annex III requirements (harmonised standards give a presumption of conformity), draw up the technical file, apply the conformity procedure Article 25 sets (a notified body for Annex I, Part A categories, including machine-learning safety functions), then sign the declaration and affix the CE marking. Until 20 January 2027 the Machinery Directive applies.

assess.text: The maker alone for most machinery (module A); a notified body for Annex I, Part A categories and, by choice, for others. National market surveillance authorities enforce it.

urml.text: A ready EU rulebook with the regulation's own citations: programs wait until the risk assessment, the substantial-modification check, the conformity procedure, the declaration, the technical file and the safety-software inventory are on record. Its obligations say why URML is not a safety component (Annex II, point 18) and never prevents a stop. Combine it with the machinery-safety template for the harmonised standards. URML takes no part in the conformity assessment.

entries.name: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689
entries.title: The EU AI Act
entries.who_short: Anyone in the EU whose robot takes its programs from an AI system
entries.what: The EU law for AI systems, as amended by the Digital Omnibus on AI (Regulation (EU) 2026/1744). For robots, machinery is now in Section B of its Annex I, so a high-risk AI safety component is assessed through the Machinery Regulation, with AI requirements added to its Annex III by 2 August 2028. AI literacy, the prohibited practices and the duty to tell people they deal with an AI system already apply.
entries.why: A robot that takes instructions in plain language through a language model is an AI system in the EU. Whether that model is a safety component decides whether the robot's AI is high-risk.
entries.who: Integrators and operators of robots driven by AI systems, and the providers of the models.
entries.how: Assess whether the AI system is a safety component (Article 6(1a) and (1b)). If it is, assess it in the machine's conformity assessment under the Machinery Regulation. Either way, tell people they deal with an AI system, support your staff's AI literacy and avoid the prohibited practices.

text.label: Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, the Digital Omnibus on AI (EUR-Lex)

assess.text: No AI Act certificate for robots. A high-risk AI safety component goes through the machine's conformity assessment, with a notified body where the Machinery Regulation requires one. The EU AI Office and national authorities oversee the rest.

urml.text: A ready EU rulebook with the Act's own citations, for a robot whose programs a model proposes through the LLM bridge: programs wait until the safety-component assessment, how people are told they deal with an AI system, and the AI literacy measures are on record. A robot with no AI system declares so and the rulebook switches off. Every program a model proposes passes the validator before it runs, which is the argument the integrator's assessment rests on.

entries.name: Regulation (EU) 2024/2847
entries.title: The EU Cyber Resilience Act
entries.who_short: Anyone selling a robot, or robot software, in the EU
entries.what: The EU law for the cybersecurity of products with digital elements, robots and their software included. It sets essential cybersecurity requirements and vulnerability handling for a support period, and applies from 11 December 2027; reporting of actively exploited vulnerabilities has applied since 11 September 2026.
entries.why: A connected robot sold in the EU needs it for its CE marking from December 2027, and its maker must already report exploited vulnerabilities within 24 hours.
entries.who: Robot makers and importers, makers of software sold for robots, and anyone who integrates third-party software into a robot they sell.
entries.how: Assess the cybersecurity risks, design to Annex I, draw up a software bill of materials, set and publish a support period, run a vulnerability disclosure process, apply the Article 32 conformity procedure (a notified body or a certification scheme for some important and all critical products), then sign the declaration of conformity, a single one with the Machinery Regulation.

assess.text: The maker for most products (module A); a notified body or a European cybersecurity certification scheme for important products that do not use harmonised standards and for critical ones. ENISA and national CSIRTs receive the vulnerability reports.

urml.text: A ready EU rulebook with the Regulation's own citations: programs wait until the product class, the conformity procedure, the cybersecurity risk assessment, the software bill of materials, the support period, the vulnerability contact and the declaration are on record. Its obligations cover 24-hour reporting, URML as a third-party component, and secure connections; the URML MQTT runtimes support TLS and broker credentials.

entries.name: 14 CFR Part 107 and Part 89
entries.title: Small drones in the US
entries.who_short: Anyone flying a drone for work in the US
entries.what: The FAA's rules for small unmanned aircraft in the US, operating rules (Part 107) and Remote ID (Part 89).
entries.why: It is federal law for commercial drone flights.
entries.who: Anyone flying a small drone for work in the US, and drone makers (Remote ID).
entries.how: The remote pilot passes the FAA's knowledge test for a remote pilot certificate, the aircraft is registered and broadcasts Remote ID, and operations outside the rules need a waiver or authorization.

assess.text: The FAA issues pilot certificates, registrations, waivers and authorizations.

urml.text: The bundled Part 107 rulebook, on by default for aircraft: altitude, speed and over-people limits, one aircraft per pilot, Remote ID declared, and the rules no static check can see as obligations. A refusal is not a legal determination.

entries.name: NDAA Section 889, FCC Covered List, DCMA Blue List
entries.title: US supply-chain rules
entries.who_short: Vendors to the US government and its contractors
entries.what: NDAA Section 889 bars federal agencies and their contractors from certain telecommunications and video-surveillance equipment, and later NDAAs extend similar limits to drones. The FCC Covered List names equipment the FCC no longer authorizes. The Blue List of drones cleared for Department of Defense use, formerly DIU's Blue UAS list, is now managed by DCMA.
entries.why: It decides who can sell robots and drones to the US government and its contractors.
entries.who: Vendors to federal agencies and contractors, and anyone whose customers are.
entries.how: Know and document where every critical component comes from, make the contract representations, and for the Blue List go through DCMA's review.

assess.text: Contracting officers, the FCC and DCMA.

urml.text: The bundled compliance policy, on by default for urml validate, checks the component origins a manifest declares. It is not legal advice and not a procurement determination.

groups.title: URML's own
groups.intro: What the URML project itself offers. Neither is a safety or compliance certification.

entries.name: URML-Certified
entries.title: Conformance to the URML specification
entries.who_short: Makers of third-party URML runtimes
entries.what: A certification that a third-party runtime conforms to the URML specification for its profiles (RFC-0705), for at most 366 days. The Licensor charges for the certification run, never for the result (RFC-0708).
entries.why: A buyer can tell that a runtime's conformance claim was reproduced by someone other than its authors.
entries.who: Makers of URML runtimes for their robots or substrates.
entries.how: Pass the full conformance suite with your own adapter, publish the package, order a certification run, and the Licensor reproduces the run offline from the public package.

assess.text: The Licensor, Yahalomik Ltd., through the URML registry, as a paid validation service quoted per run. A failed run keeps its fee and grants nothing. It certifies conformance only, never safety, security or compliance.

urml.text: URML's own program. The registry checker enforces every criterion except the attestation, and the Licensor's certification run is public code: run python -m urml_conformance.reproduce on your entry before you apply and see exactly what the Licensor will see.

entries.name: Evidence reports
entries.title: One page of evidence per deployment
entries.area: Evidence for all of the above
entries.who_short: Integrators, auditors, buyers
entries.what: Not a certification. urml evidence build writes one report per robot deployment that marks every item checked, declared, runtime, missing or outside, and regroups the rules by the standard each cites (RFC-0707).
entries.why: It shows, for every entry above that a deployment cites, what URML checks and what someone else must cover.
entries.who: Integrators before commissioning, auditors and certification bodies, buyers and insurers.
entries.how: Build it yourself and rebuild it to check it, or ask the Licensor for a reviewed report.

assess.text: Anyone can rebuild a report from the same files and compare bytes; a Licensor-reviewed report can be signed.

urml.text: The command, a worked example for auditors, and paid reviewed reports.
